$comment: Every `#[expect(lint)]` in the Rust workspace, counted per crate per lint, held from both sides by tools/arch-lint's expect-ledger.test.ts: a new expectation fails until it is listed here with a reason, and an entry whose count no longer matches fails too, so the ledger only shrinks by deletion. A site with two lints counts once for each. The reason is why the lint is wrong FOR THAT CLASS of site; the site's own `reason = "..."` says why for the one expression. A lint the workspace should instead satisfy belongs in the code, not here.

entries.reason: the count-from-f64 reads, range-checked whole and non-negative on the line before: one in the export's decoder, one in tests/recorded_oracle.rs reading the recording
an answer's length converted to the f64 the wire carries; far below 2^53
the same count-from-f64 reads as cast_possible_truncation: checked non-negative first
the fake measurer's `text.length` is a UTF-16 unit count converted to the double the TypeScript multiplies; a count under 2^53 is exact, which no string a process can hold exceeds
`f64::midpoint` avoids the overflow `(a + b) / 2` has, which the TypeScript does not; the sketch ink's control point reads `2 * mid - (a + b) / 2` and is held to its bits

the digest's free-region grid counts cells as doubles the way the TypeScript does, and a u32 index is made once from a double already known to be a whole number in 0..=250_000 (the cell budget, or a clamped span inside it)
the same cell count read as cast_possible_truncation: clamped to zero or above before the one conversion

index arithmetic in the grid search and the min-heap whose bound is an invariant the surrounding code enforces (a state index is below 2 * MAX_GRID_CELLS, a child index is compared against len first); each site names it

a value known to be 0..=1023 narrowed to the integer the TypeScript's bit arithmetic works in (one more in tests/crossing_sweep_properties.rs, whose oracle keys a small quantized test coordinate as an integer)
a count or index becomes the f64 the TypeScript works in, where JavaScript's own number has the same 2^53 ceiling and every such count is far below it
the same narrowing as cast_possible_truncation: the value is 0..=1023

the TypeScript compares coordinates with === and the port must agree on exactly the same equalities; an epsilon here would change which edges count as aligned (one more each in tests/grid_route_optimality.rs, whose reference compares grid lines the same way, tests/ink_properties.rs, whose oracle skips an axis-aligned segment the same way, tests/crossing_sweep_properties.rs, whose integer-quantized scores the sweep owes the scan exactly, tests/edge_rules_properties.rs, whose costs are exact integers, and tests/edge_routing_properties.rs, whose route coordinates the TypeScript compares with toBe, and tests/survivors_config_score.rs, whose costs and accounts are exact integers)
f64::midpoint avoids the overflow (a + b) / 2 has, and the TypeScript's expression overflows where midpoint would not; the port reproduces the TypeScript bit for bit

the same vendored module and the same reason: positions and counts the tokenizer built itself, where an overflow is a defect the fuzz target and the totality property are run to find (the release profile has overflow checks on). The arithmetic this crate's own code does on a count it was handed (`limits.rs`, `lib.rs`, the budget) is saturating and is held to the lint

the cost test times a parse with `Instant::now`, the one clock read in the crate and in a test only: a loop that spends no fuel is invisible to the count of units a parse reports, and only the clock sees it (an edit map that scanned its entries per edit spent as many units as a fast one and took 108 s over 64 KB)
the same `Instant` in the same helper, named by its type as well as by its constructor
the state and event names repeat their enum's (`Content`'s `Content` variant, the `...State` names) because they are the upstream vocabulary; a rename would orphan every comparison with upstream

the vendored tokenizer, resolvers and tree builder index events and bytes by positions they computed themselves (`vendored/mod.rs`, one expectation for the whole module). The panic freedom this lint exists for is held by what it cannot see: the `markdown_parse` fuzz target, `tests/totality.rs`'s property over documents of the tokens that decide how markdown parses, and the recorded OKF bodies of `tests/okf_corpus.rs`. The slices that took an input-derived range (`Slice`, the tree builder's stack) are `get`s that answer nothing instead
the tokenizer's state and the tree builder's context hold one flag per thing a construct tracks, as upstream; splitting them would move fields between structs and change no behaviour
the tree builder's reference record names its fields after what a reference is (`reference_kind`), as upstream
`ToString` on a node is how the tree builder flattens a label's children into the text its reference carries; it is not a `Display`, which a node does not have, as upstream

the upstream state machine and tree builder are long functions by design (`state::call` is one match arm per state, 400 lines); they are kept as they are so a later upstream fix can be compared against them, and arch-lint's function-size ledger records each one
a text run's presence-only flags (emphasis, strong, code, deleted, truncated, overflows) mirror the vocabulary's fields one for one; a flags struct would be a second spelling of the same six words
a fuzz target's own bounded count read, range-checked on the line before
the same count read as cast_possible_truncation: checked non-negative first
the prelude's runner reports a failed property the way every test fails, by panicking with the shrunk counterexample
harden-check's report holds one flag per independent mitigation, read and printed one by one; a state enum would hide which mitigation failed
